title: Green mosques
hookLine: mosques going solar and saving water

lines: THE SUN SETS THE PRAYER TIMES.
cards: A row of solar panels on a mosque roof, tilted toward the sun. There's a neat fit in that.
The same sun already runs the building's day: dawn, noon, afternoon, sunset, nightfall, every prayer time set by where it sits in the sky. Now it lights the lamps too.
Downstairs, in the washing area, someone has fitted slower taps and piped the used water out to the garden.

teach.b: Start with the word mosque. The Arabic is masjid, a place of sajdah, of bowing the forehead to the ground. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari widens it.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, lists things given to him, and one is this: the earth has been made for me a masjid and a means of purification. The whole earth, a place to pray.
So a mosque building is, in a sense, a small roofed piece of a much larger mosque, and caring for the ground outside isn't a different job from caring for the carpet inside. Second, water.
Before prayer comes wudu: washing the hands, face and arms, wiping the head, washing the feet.

teach.h: WUDU WITH A MUDD OF WATER.
teach.b: Anas reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet did his wudu with a mudd, a small measure of water, and bathed with just a few of those measures.
A report in Sunan Ibn Majah, though its chain is debated, has him see a companion using a lot of water and ask what this excess is. Can there be excess in wudu? the companion asks.
Yes, comes the answer, even if you are at a flowing river. Third, what that looks like now.
Some mosques have put panels on their roofs, swapped open taps for slower ones at the wudu stations, or collected the washing water to irrigate gardens. Some plant trees in the courtyard for shade.
None of this is a new law. It's an old instinct, the earth as a place of prayer and water used with care, meeting new tools.

how: Some mosques install solar panels, fit water-saving taps at their wudu stations, or reuse washing water for gardens, and imams sometimes remind worshipers to use little water in wudu, following the Prophet's practice.

o: mosques painted and tiled in green, a color long linked with Islam
mosques built under a new law requiring solar power and gardens
mosques that save power and water: panels, slower taps, shade trees

games.q: the green mosque — tap the pairs.
p: a place of bowing to the ground
made a masjid and a means of purification
a small measure of water for wudu

s: the hadith in al-Bukhari says only the mosque building is a place of prayer
it says the earth has been made a masjid and a means of purification.
Anas reports the Prophet did wudu with a small measure of water
a mudd for wudu, and just a few of those measures for a full bath.
green mosques follow a new religious law
no new law: an old instinct, care for the earth and for water, meeting new tools.

games.q: you're doing wudu beside a flowing river. there's endless water. is there such a thing as using too much?
o: no: it's a river, so it doesn't matter.
yes: even at a flowing river, says the report.
games.why: in the report in Ibn Majah, whose chain is debated, the answer is yes, even at a flowing river. care with water doesn't depend on shortage.

practice: Bring to mind a shared place where people gather, a mosque, a church, a temple, a hall, and walk through it slowly: the roof, the lights, the taps, the patch of ground out front.
Notice where water runs, where power hums, where something could grow. If you pray, hold the hadith in mind: the earth made a place of prayer.

wordCard.voice: Green mosques. Buildings that save power and water, drawing on a hadith that calls the whole earth a masjid, and on wudu done with a little water. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a mosque, a place of sajdah, bowing the forehead to the ground.

carryVoice: Your line: mosques going green. The building is a small piece of a much larger mosque. See you tomorrow.
